# What is an exchange?

*You'll need nothing before this chapter. It defines the order book, orders, matching, fills, the position limit,
profit and the data an exchange publishes, which every later chapter uses.*

## The story

The Varde rehearsal's first upload (chapter 1) scored €110.21 on its first public session. The portal showed totals
and a file of fills, and the session rebuilt the rest by hand. The portal's own scoring code, run on the same bot,
shows where the number comes from. It is two large numbers that nearly cancel
[(`data/sessions.csv`, from the rehearsal portal's own scoring)]{.src}:

- **cash: −€2,814.63.** Over the session the bot spent more on buying than it received from selling, fees included.
- **the position, valued: +€2,924.84.** At the end it still held what it had bought and not sold, 17 lots net across
  its products, and the portal valued them at its *settlement price*, the price it chooses for what is still held.
- **the score: €110.21,** their sum.

![The score's two parts in each of the Varde rehearsal's three public sessions. Data: `data/sessions.csv`, from
`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/private/portal.py`'s scoring of the uploaded bot.](../figures/f03_score_parts.png){#fig-score
fig-alt="Bar chart: in each session, cash and the position's value are hundreds to thousands of euros apart and of opposite sign, and the score, their sum, is between 110 and 137 euros."}

All three sessions are in @fig-score. In the third the signs flip: €5,486.92 of cash against a short position worth
−€5,366.09, for a score of €120.83. In every session the score is a small difference between two numbers, and one of
them depends on a price the portal chose. The session didn't know which: valuing the positions at each session's last
mid gave €369.67 against the portal's €367.61, close enough to use and not exact
[(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/results/HANDOVER.md`, "Portal against local")]{.src}. The answer key says
the portal used the average price of each product's last 100 trades, weighted by size. Hold that thought: it is why the end of a
session matters more than any single tick, and why chapter 10 counts the price used to value a position among a
backtest's assumptions.

## The idea

### The order book

An exchange is a place where offers to trade wait until someone takes them. Each offer is a *limit order*: buy up to
this many *lots* (units of the product, the smallest quantity it trades in) at this price or
lower, or sell up to this many at this price or higher. The offers waiting at a moment
make up the *order book*: the *bids* (offers to buy) on one side, the *asks* (offers to sell) on the other, each side
grouped into *levels*, one per price (@fig-book).

![One tick of Prosperity 3's Kelp, round 1, day 0. Data: `data/order_book.csv`, from the engine's loader.](../figures/f02_order_book.png){#fig-book
fig-alt="An order book: bids of 2 lots at 2,029 and 23 lots at 2,028; asks of 6 lots at 2,030 and 25 lots at 2,032; the mid 2,029.5 and the wall mid 2,030."}

The highest bid is the *best bid* (2,029 here); the lowest ask is the *best ask* (2,030). Together they are the
*touch*, and the gap between them is the *spread*, here 1 credit. Prices move in fixed steps, the *tick size*: 1
credit on Prosperity, 5 cents on the Varde Exchange. A spread of one tick is as narrow as a book can be. The word *tick* has a second sense, which the book also uses:
one step of the market's clock, one snapshot of the book and one call of the bot; the context says which. Halfway
across the touch is the *mid*, 2,029.5. Chapter 3 is about why the mid is often the wrong number to trust, and what
the large orders at 2,028 and 2,032, the *walls*, tell you instead.

### Taking and making

A new order either crosses the book or it doesn't.

- A **buy at or above the best ask** (or a sell at or below the best bid) *crosses*. It trades at once with the
  waiting orders, at their prices, best first, until it is filled or the next level is beyond its own price. This is
  *taking*, and the order is *aggressive*: you pay the spread for trading now.
- An order that **doesn't cross** joins the book and waits. This is *making*, or quoting, and the order is
  *passive*: you offer liquidity and hope someone takes it. When they do, your order is *filled*, at your price.

A trade between two other participants is a *print*, and the side that crossed is its *aggressor*. Chapters 4 and 5
are about why the passive side earns the spread on average, and when it doesn't.

### Matching in full

The rule that decides who trades with whom is the exchange's *matching*. Nearly every exchange uses *price-time
priority*: an incoming order trades first with the best price on the other side, and among orders at the same price,
with the one that arrived first. So a waiting order has a place in a *queue*. Joining a busy level means waiting
behind everyone already there, and you move up only as the orders ahead of you trade or are cancelled. Prosperity's
own glossary says its exchange enforces exactly this
[(`references/prosperity-wikis/prosperity4/trading-glossary-d14f71.md:69`)]{.src}.

On Prosperity, though, the queue hardly exists, because nothing waits long enough to be in one. Our engine follows
its rules, checked fill for fill against the open-source backtester [(`python/arena/engine.py`, the module's
docstring; `ARCHITECTURE.md`, "Matching rules (Prosperity semantics)")]{.src}:

1. Every tick the bot sees the book and returns orders.
2. If a product's orders could take its position past the limit, every order for that product is rejected (below).
3. Each order trades against the visible book at the book's prices, best price first.
4. What's left can fill against that tick's prints, at the order's own price.
5. Anything still unfilled is cancelled. No order rests into the next tick.

Rule 4 is the one a replay has to guess at, because the prints happened between other bots: whether a print at our
price would have come to us is the *fill model*, and chapter 10 is about how much rides on it. Rule 5 is the likely
reason one Prosperity 4 team's probe found "no queueing": orders at the best price were served regardless of when
they were placed (*their claim*) [(`references/online-snapshots/Leo-Hawking_IMC-Prosperity-4-Review.README.md:204`)]{.src}.

Most other exchanges, and all four of our rehearsals, let orders **rest** until they are filled or cancelled. The
engine's resting mode replaces rule 5 with an exchange where they do [(`python/arena/engine.py`)]{.src}:

- What doesn't trade at once rests at its price, at the back of its level's queue: the volume the book already shows
  there is ahead of it. An order marked *immediate-or-cancel* doesn't rest.
- Prints at its price first use up the volume ahead of it, then fill it. A print through its price fills it at once,
  since it would have traded first.
- If a later book shows the other side at or through its price, those orders would have hit it, and it fills at its
  own price.
- The queue moves up when the level shrinks by more than the prints explain, because orders ahead were cancelled; how
  much of that happens ahead of us is a guess (chapter 10).
- The bot's own orders never trade with each other.

Each exchange then adds its own details. The Varde Exchange applied a step's cancels before its new orders, took at
most 10 actions a step, had no immediate-or-cancel orders, and filled resting orders only from prints, best price
then oldest first [(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/public/rules.md`, "Your bot" and "Matching")]{.src}. The
Kestrel Bourse allowed 6 actions a step, cancels included, and 3 working orders a product. Each of those is a line in the format's engine
settings, and a line the bot's adapter has to respect.

### One order, worked through

Take the book of @fig-book, at timestamp 400, and send one order: buy 10 Kelp at 2,031
[(`data/worked_order.csv`, from `arena.engine.run_day`)]{.src}.

- The order crosses: 2,031 is above the best ask of 2,030. It takes the 6 lots there, at 2,030, the book's price, not
  its own. The next ask, 2,032, is above its price, so the taking stops.
- Four lots are left at 2,031, the highest bid in the book now and alone at their price.
- Under Prosperity's rules, no print that tick reaches 2,031, so the four lots are cancelled. The bot bought 6.
- With orders resting, the four lots wait. At the next tick, 500, the book's best ask has dropped to 2,031, at our
  price: those sellers would have traded with our bid, so it fills, 4 lots at 2,031.

The same order, the same data, two exchanges: 6 lots or 10. Nothing in the recording says which happened, only the
rules do.

### Position limits, and how exchanges enforce them

Your *position* in a product is what you hold: positive after buying more than you sold (*long*), negative after
selling more than you bought (*short*; the exchanges in these competitions let you sell what you don't hold). Each
product has a *position limit*, and how it is enforced differs more than you would guess.

- **Prosperity** rejects the whole tick for a product. If all of a tick's buy orders for Kelp, filled, could take the
  position past 50, or all its sells past −50, every Kelp order that tick is rejected, the sells with the buys
  [(`ARCHITECTURE.md`, "Matching rules (Prosperity semantics)", rule 2)]{.src}. A bot that quotes its whole room on
  both sides can lose all its orders for a tick by miscounting one lot.
- **The Varde Exchange** did the same, counting what already rests: if a step's new orders could pass the limit, all
  that step's new orders for the product were rejected, while the resting ones stayed
  [(`python/experiments/mock_round/round4/public/rules.md`, "Limits, fees and errors")]{.src}.
- **The Halden Exchange** checked each order on its own, in the order the bot sent them, and rejected only the ones
  that didn't fit [(`python/experiments/mock_round/round2/public/rules.md`, "How each step is processed")]{.src}.
- **The Kestrel Bourse** rejected nothing. After every step it charged 0.25 credits for each lot of a position beyond
  its limit. The first bot to trade there didn't count the orders still on their way, overfilled its limits, and
  paid 2,191.75 credits in charges on the two hidden sessions, toward a score of −3,553 credits
  [(`data/kestrel_breach.csv`, from the round's `portal.py hidden`)]{.src}.
- **AlgoTrade 2026**, a live competition in Zagreb whose rules, one team's code and its recorded data are in
  `references/`, set different limits for each side: 2,000 units long, 200 short
  [(`references/algotrade2026-pitfa19/.firecrawl/algotrade-api.md:687-688`)]{.src}.

A rule that rejects is a cliff, and a rule that charges is a slope. Under the first the bot must never send what
could breach; under the second a breach is a cost to weigh. Chapter 10 shows the cliff's worst case, orders that
arrive a tick late and are checked again against a position their own earlier fills have moved.

### Profit and loss

*PnL* is what a bot would have if it closed everything now:

::: {.eq speak="profit is the cash, plus the position times the price it is valued at"}
$$\text{PnL} = \text{cash} + \text{position} \times \text{price}$$
:::

Cash goes down by the price of everything bought and up by everything sold; fees come out of it. The price that
values the position is the *mark*: our engine's default is the mid, Prosperity's own data carries one, and the
Varde portal used its 100-trade average [(`python/arena/engine.py`, `--mark`)]{.src}. The story's identity is this formula,
session by session.

### What the data looks like

Every exchange records the same market differently, and the repo meets three shapes (@fig-shapes).

![The three shapes of exchange data, each read by its format plug-in into the engine's one form, a `Day` of `Tick`s.
The samples are real rows: Prosperity 3's Kelp at timestamps 400 and 500, the Varde rehearsal's first steps; the event
log is illustrative. Diagram; the types from `python/arena/model.py`.](../figures/g02_data_shapes.png){#fig-shapes
fig-alt="Three boxes on the left, snapshots from Prosperity, prints with an aggressor flag from the Varde rehearsal, and an event log, each with sample rows, feed three plug-ins, Prosperity's, the Varde round's own and the event-log skeleton, which all produce one box, a Day of Ticks, each tick holding a timestamp, a book per product, the trades per product and a mark per product; it feeds the engine and every tool."}

- **Snapshots** (Prosperity): one row per tick and product with three levels a side, 10,000 ticks a day, and a
  separate file of the trades between ticks, with buyer and seller names when the round reveals them. The plug-in
  reads each row as a tick's book and joins the trades to it by timestamp.
- **Prints with an aggressor flag** (the Varde Exchange): one line per step holding the book and the step's prints,
  each marked with the side that crossed. The plug-in keeps the flag by naming the crossing side `taker` in the
  trade's buyer or seller field, so a tool can ask who was in a hurry.
- **An event log** (LOBSTER, and many real exchanges' own feeds): every order added, changed, cancelled or executed,
  by id. The plug-in replays the events and takes the book as it stands after each step as a tick, so any snapshot
  can be rebuilt from it. (Our LOBSTER and ABIDES days are converted into Prosperity's layout before they are loaded.)

Whatever the shape, the plug-in's `load_days` returns the same thing: a `Day`, with its products, limits and
per-product facts such as the tick size, and its `Tick`s, each with a timestamp, a `Book` of bids and asks per
product, the prints, and the prices to value positions at [(`python/arena/model.py`; `python/arena/formats/`)]{.src}.
The engine and every tool work on that, never on the exchange's own files. That is why a new exchange on the day
costs a plug-in and an adapter, not a new set of tools, and why the Varde session had its plug-in written three
minutes in.

### Reading a claim about the book

A book shows a few levels. Is that the market? A team in AlgoTrade 2026 looked at where trades printed on one of its
exchanges, ZSE, and found "53.9% of all ZSE trades print outside the visible top-3", which they read as the exchange's
own market maker quoting at levels 4 and 5 [(`references/algotrade2026-pitfa19/analysis/mm_analysis.md:153`)]{.src}.
Two things in their own files change what that number means. It came from the 3,115 prints they had when they wrote
it (*their claim*) [(`mm_analysis.md:43`)]{.src}. And "visible" meant visible in their recording, which kept three
levels a side, while the exchange sent every team five
[(`mm_analysis.md:48-49`; `.firecrawl/algotrade-api.md:518-546`)]{.src}. So what they measured was mostly what their
recorder dropped, not depth that nobody could see.

We re-ran their test on the 1.4 million prints committed with their analysis. Each print against the last recorded
snapshot before it gives 34.0%, from 12 to 21% on the exchange-traded funds to 48% on one stock. But a book moves
between snapshots: counting only prints outside both the snapshot before and the one after gives 5.7%
[(`data/hidden_depth.csv`, from the committed data)]{.src}. Neither number says how deep the real book was, because
the recording can't. On Prosperity 3's round 1, whose data is what the bots were shown, a similar check, against the
books before and at each print, finds no print outside the levels shown, on any of its three products; 3.4 to 3.8%
of its trades hit a price with no shown level, about half of them inside the spread [(`data/hidden_depth.csv`;
`experiments.day.structure --data p3 --days 1 --sections fingerprints`)]{.src}. The lesson is about reading, not
about depth. Before trusting a figure, ask what sample it came from and what the data it was measured on left out.
And a number from someone's write-up is a claim until it is re-run.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
The order book is the state, a tick is a time step, and the bot is a policy from state to actions; the format plug-in
is a data loader that maps every source to one schema. Where the analogy breaks: the state is partly made of other
agents' intentions, which change when you act, and a replay freezes them (chapter 10). The environment's transition
rules, matching and limits, differ between exchanges in ways that matter more than most model choices, and they are
given in prose, not code. And the reward, PnL, is defined only after a choice of price for what you hold, like a
metric that needs a reference you have to pick.
:::
